headline: Brad Jacobs describes the 2015 acquisition of Conway as an out-of-consensus call that doubled EBIT in two years and proved to be a career-defining deal for XPO.
reasoning: XPO originally sought to acquire Menlo's contract logistics subsidiary for cross-sell opportunities, but when that structure fell apart, Conway approached XPO about buying the whole company. Despite XPO being primarily an asset-light brokerage, Jacobs saw a major cost-reduction opportunity because Conway had completed three large acquisitions without integrating them — leaving three HR departments, three IT departments, and three sales organisations. Wall Street reacted badly and the stock fell sharply, but Jacobs stood by the thesis, telling the Wall Street Journal it would be the best deal of his career. Over time the operating ratio improved dramatically toward the 70s from 96%, and EBIT doubled within two years, vindicating the out-of-consensus call.
quote: I wanted it real bad because they had these really blue chip customers. And I wanted to cross sell into those customers... the Conway folks said, why don't you look at buying the whole company? I said, wow, it's an interesting idea. I had never really thought about buying an LTL trucking company... as we looked at it and studied, wow, there's a lot of costs we can take out of this because they had done three big acquisitions and never integrated them. So, they had three HR departments, three IT departments, three sales organizations, three of everything... I remember being interviewed by the Wall Street Journal. The stock had come down a lot. And I told the reporter, I think it's going to be the best deal of my career so far... it turned out I was right.
episode_title: Brad Jacobs: Question Deeply, Act Quickly

sector: Highway / Road Infrastructure / Traffic Control Rental
headline: Brad Jacobs concedes that concentrating United Rentals investment around the 21st Century Transportation Act was a costly mistake, resulting in approximately $500 million of losses.
reasoning: Around the turn of the century, US Congress passed legislation promising large-scale spending on bridges, tunnels, and roads. Jacobs responded by acquiring five or six of the largest traffic-control rental companies — cones, barricades, striping — to dominate what he expected to be a booming market. The anticipated government spending never materialised, leaving the acquisitions stranded and forcing a write-off of approximately $500 million. In hindsight, Jacobs says he should not have concentrated so heavily on a single policy-dependent catalyst — a 'stroke of the pen' risk — and that the lesson was not to 'bet the ranch' on any single legislative or macro outcome.
quote: There was this act that came out in Congress, the transportation something act of the 21st century, and they were going to spend all this money to reconstruct the bridges and the tunnels and the roads in America. I was in United Rentals at the time. So I said, I got to buy all the rental companies for all that orange stuff on the barricades and cones and striping. I said, I got to dominate that market. So I bought five or six of the biggest ones... I was like waiting for all the money. The money never came. So Congress never really spent the money... We probably lost 500 million bucks. So it's a lot of money and you remember that forever.
episode_title: Brad Jacobs: Question Deeply, Act Quickly

headline: Acquisition described as best deal yet, citing massive cross-sell synergies across hundreds of thousands of combined customers
reasoning: XPO/QXO acquired TopBuild, which does both distribution and installation of building products, representing a strategic pivot from a pure distribution model. Jacobs acknowledges the market has not yet fully appreciated the deal, making it another out-of-consensus call. The combined entity has around 200,000 customers, and early analysis already indicates significant untapped cross-sell potential — for instance, TopBuild serves data centres with insulation but those same customers buy many other products XPO sells from third parties. On the procurement side, the combined group now exceeds $1 billion of spend with a number of shared vendor partners, creating meaningful purchasing leverage. Jacobs calls it his best deal yet and says momentum in the organisation is strong.
quote: We also worked on something more recently with TopBuild... That's an out of consensus call because we were mainly doing distribution of installation and now we bought a company that does both distribution and installation. So it was a little bit of a pivot again and the market hasn't yet fully appreciated how good the deal is. I think it's going to be my best deal yet... now together we've got something like a couple hundred thousand customers... TopBuild is a lot of insulation for data centers. Well, data centers buy every single thing we sell other than windows. Cause they don't like windows. So we got to penetrate that. So there's a big, big cross-sell opportunity there.

headline: Sees AI as a near-term operational positive for corporates but warns of longer-term existential and geopolitical risks that 'scare the hell' out of him
reasoning: Jacobs describes AI as a significant short-term productivity enhancer for CEOs — meeting notes, data analysis, CRM sentiment analysis and word clouds are now delivered same-day rather than in three months. For a company with 1,150 locations, AI allows real-time aggregation of information from across the organisation that was previously impractical. However, he is genuinely frightened about longer-term scenarios including rogue AI, adversaries leapfrogging the US in cyber, bio, or nuclear AI applications, and inequitable distribution of AI-driven economic gains. He says he tries to lean positive but acknowledges the uncertainty is real and serious.
quote: I as a CEO am so much more effective now with AI because I get all the meeting notes and information is collected and analyzed and summarized like same day. These things that used to get to me in three months, if they even got to me... One of your big challenges when you're running a company is you have all these offices, we have 1150 locations now. How do you know what's going on in all that? And AI now is grabbing all this information... I mean, it's really amazing. You can get so much more done in so much less time... If we end up utilizing AI in a responsible way and we're able to mind the earth's resources and share it equitably and fairly and eliminate poverty and eliminate ill health and people live long periods of time and we get along with each other. That'd be great if on the other hand, AI goes crazy on us and goes rogue and gets a mind of its own... That's not going to be good. So I try to remain positive about it, but I'm scared about it.
episode_title: Brad Jacobs: Question Deeply, Act Quickly

headline: EQT's Jean Salata highlights Nord Anglia Education as a flagship success, growing from $300-400M to over $14B enterprise value through a roll-up strategy across 90+ international schools.
reasoning: Salata identified Nord Anglia Education as an out-of-consensus opportunity in 2007-2008 when for-profit education in Asia was not on investors' radar. The firm acquired the business for $300-400M total enterprise value when it operated six schools, attracted by a fragmented industry ripe for M&A roll-up, a recurring and prepaid tuition revenue model with strong cash flow, and the ability to leverage BPEA's Asian network to help a UK-listed company penetrate Asian markets. Over 15 years across subsequent funds and vehicles, EQT grew the portfolio to over 90 schools globally and recently transacted at over $14 billion enterprise value. The investment also demonstrated the value of control ownership in navigating crises including the GFC and COVID.
quote: We took the time, it was a business with six schools, bought it for something like $300 or $400 million at the time in total enterprise value. And over the last sort of 15 years, we've owned subsequent funds and vehicles, and we've taken it now to over 90 schools around the world. And we just recently transacted on the asset at over $14 billion enterprise value. A reasonable return, I think. But looking at new sectors and how you can tackle deal constructs that are a little bit different, I think is a way to generate some alpha in our industry.
episode_title: Jean Eric Salata: Find the Comeback in the Setback

headline: EQT admits early India strategy of minority, opportunistic investments failed due to governance weaknesses and lack of sector focus — a key thesis revision that reshaped the firm's entire Asian strategy.
reasoning: In the early 2000s, BPEA entered India through a broad range of minority investments across many industries, which largely failed. Key failure modes included governance issues, inability to influence management quality as a minority holder, illiquidity, and legal challenges from portfolio company founders exploiting the firm's weak minority position. The lesson prompted a full strategic pivot toward control investments and sector concentration in IT services, and an emphasis on professional management teams. This experience directly informed the broader EQT philosophy of control ownership and active value creation.
quote: What we were doing wrong, we had the wrong strategies. And when we changed subsequently, it was number one, we stopped making minority investments because we felt like it was very important to have control. We had issues with governance. We had issues with management quality in the businesses and not being able to do anything about it. We had issues without getting liquidity in our investments, being stuck as a minority investor. So we shifted from minority investments to control investments. The second thing we did is that instead of being opportunistic and investing across whatever deals we found in the market, we decided, let's analyze this top down. Let's look at the market. Let's try to understand where the biggest growth is going to happen and where the best private equity type opportunities are going to exist and where the most controlled deals are going to exist.
episode_title: Jean Eric Salata: Find the Comeback in the Setback

headline: EQT views AI as a tailwind for the education sector, contrasting with value-destructive impacts seen in other industries.
reasoning: Salata argues that AI's impact is highly sector- and sub-sector-specific, not uniform. Within education specifically, he views AI as a tailwind. The firm's approach is to ensure portfolio companies have the right leadership team and an AI strategy executed with urgency, warning that firms slow to adapt risk disruption from incumbents or AI-native entrants.
quote: I think in education specifically, AI is a tailwind. The way we're looking overall at AI is it's very sector specific and we're not going to be uniform. Even within sectors, it's within sub-sectors and certain companies, there will be value creation as a result of AI and others there will be value destruction as a result of AI. So what we're really focused on now is making sure we have the right leadership team, making sure everybody has an AI strategy, and then we have the right leadership team to execute on that strategy with a sense of urgency. Because if you don't move quickly here to take advantage of whatever AI offers to your particular company or your industry, then other either incumbents or with the worst AI native players will be coming in to really disrupt your business.
episode_title: Jean Eric Salata: Find the Comeback in the Setback

headline: EQT's Jean Salata identifies Japanese buyouts as the single biggest private equity opportunity in Asia today, driven by corporate governance reforms and conglomerate restructuring.
reasoning: Salata describes the Japanese buyout market as the standout opportunity in Asia, comparing it to the US conglomerate restructuring wave of the 1980s where businesses lacked focus and were not executing to full potential. He cites a policy tailwind from corporate governance reforms implemented by the Tokyo Stock Exchange and a growing pipeline of take-private opportunities. EQT has already made a number of investments and announced some take-privates in the market, with Salata expecting deal flow to continue to grow across the industry.
quote: I think the single biggest opportunity we see in the region today are Japanese buyouts. That market is growing. It's a market where we think there's a lot of excess return opportunities available to investors. It reminds us a lot of the sort of conglomerate days of the US in the 80s, where you had businesses that lack focus, that weren't executing to full potential. We're seeing a lot of take private opportunities there. And I think generally there's a policy tailwind in Japan related to the corporate governance reforms that have been implemented by the Tokyo Stock Exchange. We have a very active pipeline there. We've made a number of investments. We've announced some take privates recently. I think the opportunity is going to continue to generate more and more deal flow for all of our industry actually.

headline: EQT views AI as a highly disruptive but navigable force, requiring company-by-company strategic responses rather than a uniform sectoral approach.
reasoning: Salata frames AI as potentially very disruptive and challenging but contextualises it within humanity's broader history of navigating technological change. He stresses the impact will vary significantly by sector, sub-sector, and individual company, with both winners and losers. quote: Even now, if you look at AI, AI is potentially a very disruptive, very challenging, kind of scary development in the world. And so if you step back and put it into the context of, well, we've been through many changes as humanity before. We've seen technological change, disruption, war, COVID, and other sorts of calamities. But you're able to sort of navigate through these things. episode_title: Jean Eric Salata: Find the Comeback in the Setback

headline: EQT pivot to control investments in Indian IT services after early minority-stake failures transformed India into the firm's best-performing portfolio, illustrating a focused sector and governance-led strategy.
reasoning: Following early losses from a broad, opportunistic minority-investment strategy across India, Salata led a strategic overhaul: shifting exclusively to control investments in the IT services and technology sector, avoiding founder-promoter-run companies in favour of professional CEOs aligned on value creation. The firm spent two to three years rebuilding conviction and pipeline before making new investments. This restructured approach delivered a turnaround from worst to best portfolio performance in India across subsequent funds. The lesson reinforced the importance of control ownership, governance quality, and deep sector focus over opportunistic diversification.
quote: We came to the conclusion that IT services, the technology sector, was the big sector for us to be focused on. And we basically exclusively focused on that one sector for, I would say, almost 10 years. We also started really doubling down on professional management, avoiding founders or promoters, as they're called in India, and really working with kind of professional CEOs that we would bring in who were very aligned with us and driving value creation together. And it did actually take us, I'd say, another two or three, maybe even four years before we made another investment, having to reorientate ourselves... That strategy worked, and we went from having the worst performance in our portfolio in India to having the best performance in our portfolio in India in our subsequent funds.
episode_title: Jean Eric Salata: Find the Comeback in the Setback

headline: Druckenmiller calls the yield curve 'overrated' as a trading instrument, preferring outright bond directionality
reasoning: Druckenmiller says he has almost never traded the yield curve itself, preferring to take directional positions on rates going up or down outright. He describes relative value curve trades as rarely profitable on both sides simultaneously, noting that the simultaneous move of short rates down and long rates up seen recently was unusual. His view is that trading bonds outright is superior to relative value yield curve positioning.
quote: Yield curve. Overrated. Really? Yep. So we're in with the equity as a macro indicator out with the yield curve. Oh no, it's a pretty good indicator. I've never traded the yield curve much. I talked to my peers. I got the curve on. I'm like, look, rates are going to go up or they're going to go down. So when I say overrated, I'm talking about trading the yield curve as opposed to just trading bonds outright. Very rarely do you win on both sides.
